# Length-Prefixed Message Framing

TCP is a **byte stream**, not a message stream. It guarantees order and delivery and
guarantees nothing about boundaries: one `send` can arrive as three reads, and three sends
can arrive as one. Any application that exchanges messages over it must define where each
message ends.

The standard answer is to say so up front:

```
4-byte unsigned big-endian length || UTF-8 payload
```

Read exactly four bytes, decode the length, then read exactly that many. One connection
carries many frames.

## The bug this replaces

`sock.recv(4096)` and hope. It works perfectly on loopback, where messages are small and
arrive whole, and it fails in production under three conditions the developer never
reproduced: a message larger than the buffer, two messages coalesced by Nagle's algorithm,
and a message split across TCP segments by a smaller path MTU.

The variants are no better. Reading until the buffer "looks like valid JSON" makes the
parser the framer and breaks on any payload containing a nested structure. Delimiter
framing — newline, `\0` — requires escaping the delimiter in the payload, and the escaping
is what gets forgotten.

## Why the length must be bounded

An attacker-supplied length prefix is an allocation instruction. `0xFFFFFFFF` asks the
server to allocate 4 GiB before a single byte of payload arrives, and a handful of
connections doing that is a denial of service that costs the attacker twelve bytes.

So the cap comes first — 64 KiB in the implementation this is written from — and it is
checked **before** allocating, not after reading. An invalid size gets a framed error
response where that is still possible, then the connection closes, because a stream whose
framing is in doubt cannot be resynchronised: there is no way to tell payload bytes from a
length prefix once you have lost your place.

This is the same ordering discipline as verify-then-parse in
[[hmac-session-tokens-over-jwt]]. Everything after the boundary is attacker-controlled
until something trusted says otherwise.

## What HTTP does instead

HTTP solves the identical problem twice — `Content-Length`, or chunked transfer encoding —
which is why an HTTP adapter needs no framing code of its own. That is not the framing
disappearing; it is the framing living in a library. Disagreement between two
implementations about *which* of those two mechanisms applies to a request is the entire
basis of request-smuggling attacks, so "the library handles it" is a statement about where
the complexity lives, not whether it exists.

Building both transports against one contract is what makes the distinction visible: see
[[distributed-systems-protocol-labs]] and [[dual-implementation-as-cross-check]].

## Read timeouts belong here too

A peer that sends a length prefix and then nothing holds a server thread forever. Framing
code needs an idle read timeout as much as it needs a size cap — both are limits on what a
single unauthenticated connection can consume.
